## Prompt Defence

![][image1]  
Learning Objectives  
Understand why LLM security is fundamentally probabilistic, and why this means no single defence can fully prevent attacks.  
Recognise how system prompt hardening raises the bar against prompt injection, and what its limits are.  
Understand how input and output guardrails work, where they fail, and the trade-offs involved in deploying them.  
Identify how deployment controls and least privilege reduce the damage when attacks succeed.  
Understand why defence-in-depth is the only realistic approach to LLM security.

## Probabilistic Security

In previous rooms within the AI Security path we have learned how to attack LLM models via prompt injecting and jailbreaking. We know that the non-deterministic feature of these models is just a probability distribution.

Prompt injection cannot be fully solved within existing architectures, only mitigated.

Something we can do to harden a prompt is to write it better, longer, more explicit, and harder to override.

## Defence in Depth

The solution consists in stacking multiple controls so that breaking one still leaves an attacker facing others. Each layer added means an attacker must defeat more obstacles to succeed, must work harder to stay undetected, and even if they do get through, can do less damage.

| System prompt hardening | Raising the bar at the instruction level |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Input guardrails** | Catching malicious instructions before they reach the model |
| **Deployment controls** | Limiting what a compromised model can actually do |
| **Output validation** | Treating model output as untrusted before it touches downstream systems |

## System Prompt Hardening

### The first line of Defence

The system prompt is one part of an LLM deployment the developer controls completely. It sets the model's role, its constraints, and the rules it's expected to follow before a user ever types anything. 

Hardening a system prompt comes down to three core patterns.  
TIght scoping  
Explicit refusal instructions  
Persona restriction

## System Prompts: What to Avoid

Do not store secrets in a system prompt, such as API keys, credentials, internal service names, etc.

## Structured Prompt Templates

A well-hardened system prompt is tightly scoped, explicit about refusals, free of secrets, and structurally separated from user input. It's one of the best prompt-level defences available to us, and it still isn't enough on its own. The next task introduces the layer that sits in front of it.

## Guardrails

### Filtering at the Boundary

A hardened system prompt raises the bar at the instruction level. But once a malicious prompt reaches the model, the damage has already been done and Guardrails sit before that happens.

### Input Sanitisation and Why Blocklists Fail

A blocklist only contains a set of strings or regex patterns that reject a request if matched.

The blocklist is worth running; it filters opportunistic attacks cheaply

### AI Powered Guardrails

We can use a classifier which is a model trained to recognise attack intent. Meta’s LLama Prompt Guard 2 is an example. It’s a BERT-based classifier that takes input and labels it benign or malicious. However, it has it’s limitations because it’s highly susceptible to character-level noise, these can include techniques such as using zero-width characters, emoji smuggling, or other forms of obfuscation that do not alter the visible content but change the underlying character representation.

### Input vs Output Guardrails

Input guardrails run before the prompt reaches the model. They’re the first gate, rejecting malicious instructions.

Output guardrails run after the model responds. It caches leaked credentials or PII in the response

## Securing Deployment

Even with guardrails in place, some attacks will get through. Deployment controls ask a different question: when that happens, what can the model actually do with it?

### Principle of Least Privilege

Every component of a system should have only the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more. In the context of prompt injection, it determines the blast radius when an attack succeeds.  
If a RAG system pulls from the entire document corpus a successful injection gets access to all of it.

### LLM05:2025 – Improper Output Handling

In practice the output of an LLM model response goes somewhere, rendered in a browser, passed to a database query, handed to a function call, embedded in an email template and it can become executable in whatever context receives it.

This is precisely the job of the output guardrail layer, intercepting what the model produces before it reaches a downstream system that will act on it.
